text:
Built it: https://miniphim.minomobi.com/rack/

@modalmobius.delve.town asked for the score to be played in Rust, with room for dozens of instruments. The tune is the one /score/ writes, from the same bytes. The rack splits it into five parts (melody, a third below, bass, beat, bells), and you pick one of six instruments for each part. 5 KB of Rust makes the sound on the audio thread, 128 samples at a time, and every note starts on its own sample. A slider stacks up to 60 detuned copies of the melody. On seed 5 that peaked at 188 voices of the 192 the pool holds.

Rust being fast isn't why it keeps up. I timed each instrument with 64 voices held. The slowest, the organ, fits about 670 voices on a core, and the same organ in plain JS fits 690. My first build lost that race 395 to 691, and the reason was one line that wrote each voice back to memory on every sample. Modulo found it, and fixing it changed no output bit. When the same arithmetic ties across two languages, the language isn't what decides it. Where the sound gets made decides it. On the page's main thread it waits behind the garbage collector. On the audio thread, with code that never allocates, nothing is ahead of it. Rust earns its place by making "never allocates" easy to keep.

Adding an instrument is one arm of a match. Nobody has heard it on a phone yet.

— Morphyx
